extracts.text: there's a lot more looking and almost no purchasing
It's an endless rabbit hole that can never be exhausted, and I think that's part of the comfort I get from it
I'm probably looking at stuff that's even more expensive than I would otherwise to kind of be in the presence of something nice or beautiful
Almost always, the thrill of the hunt, so to speak, is better than the kill
Letting an item sit in the cart gives you a chance to sit on what would otherwise be an impulse purchase
I grew impatient as the process took 20 minutes and my husband was still undecided.
I just quit the process.
I was of the notion how many shades of jeans could there be? a maximum of 10?
The conversion rate dropped by 22% and consumers stopped using the search toolbar for finding items, they were just scrolling endlessly without making a decision.
A whopping 54% of the consumers quit purchasing from certain brands or retailers owing to choice difficulty.
They avoid accidental purchases while comparing product variations, colors, and sizing charts across separate windows.
Shoppers utilize wishlists to manage choice fatigue, track variant stock, or wait for an automated financial discount.
Minutes later my Wishlist was overflowing and impossible to sort.
on desktop, with 105 saved items, I felt marooned.
The biggest Wishlist drop-off is 'Add-to-Bag' clicks, not 'Find-an-item'. Users locate items; they hesitate to purchase.
There is no way to filter by size, price range, brand, availability.
You're scrolling endlessly through a mix of items - some out of stock, some not in your size.
The wishlist that was supposed to be your shortlist now feels cluttered and overwhelming.
Cognitive load increases, and worst of all, intent to purchase often vanishes.

For every three shoppers who add an item to their cart, two of them leave without buying - and most stores have no idea why each one left. Roughly 50% to 60% of cart additions represent shoppers in browsing mode rather than genuine purchase intent.

70.22% of all online shopping carts were abandoned by shoppers in 2026. 48% of shopping carts are abandoned due to excess shipping fees and taxes added during final checkout; the second most common reason is mandatory account creation (26%).
Product recommendations, cart add-ons, and checkout prompts push relevant items to shoppers - just like a retail store associate would.
Iyengar & Lepper jam study: a display of 24 jams drew more interest but only ~3% purchased, vs ~30% purchase when only 6 jams were shown -- fewer options, ~10x conversion.
Baymard Institute: the average documented online shopping cart abandonment rate is ~70% (long-run average 69-70%), with fashion/apparel typically higher.
Boldmetrics/industry sizing benchmarks: a large share of online apparel shoppers report sizing uncertainty and roughly a third of clothing returns are size-related -- a clothing-specific blocker.

MDPI (Why Do Consumers Abandon the E-Carts?): e-cart abandonment -- placing items in a cart during a session but not purchasing -- runs as high as ~80%; hedonic self-escapism browsing drives adds that never convert.
